questions.question: Which statement best characterizes a sparse matrix in the context of algorithm and storage design?
questions.choice_A: A matrix in which the number of nonzero entries is much smaller than the total number of entries, so algorithms and storage focus on operating only on nonzeros.
questions.choice_B: A matrix whose determinant is zero, requiring special numerical handling.
questions.choice_C: Any matrix with at least one zero in every row or column.
questions.choice_D: A matrix that is symmetric and positive definite, enabling faster solvers.

questions.question: In compressed sparse row (CSR) format, which access pattern is most efficient?
questions.choice_A: Column-wise traversal of the matrix
questions.choice_B: Row-wise traversal of the matrix, especially for matrix-vector products with a dense vector on the right
questions.choice_C: Random insertion of new nonzeros
questions.choice_D: Incremental updates to arbitrary single entries

questions.question: Which sparsity pattern is most naturally associated with a fixed small bandwidth around the main diagonal?
questions.choice_A: Block-sparse
questions.choice_B: Random sparsity
questions.choice_C: Banded sparsity
questions.choice_D: Hierarchical sparsity

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical motivation for using COO (coordinate) format during preprocessing?
questions.choice_A: Fast row-wise SpMV with contiguous memory access
questions.choice_B: Asymptotically optimal SpGEMM accumulation
questions.choice_C: Minimal storage overhead for symmetric matrices
questions.choice_D: Easy append of new (row, col, value) triplets and flexible sorting before converting to CSR/CSC

questions.question: What is the typical time complexity of multiplying a sparse matrix by a dense vector (SpMV) when using an appropriate compressed format?
questions.choice_A: $O(\text{nnz})$, where nnz is the number of nonzero entries
questions.choice_B: $O(n^2)$, where $n$ is the dimension of the matrix
questions.choice_C: $O(n\log n)$, due to sorting of indices
questions.choice_D: $O(\text{nnz} \log n)$, due to accumulation costs

questions.question: What is a primary challenge for sparse-sparse matrix multiplication (SpGEMM) compared to SpMV?
questions.choice_A: Lack of associativity in multiplication of sparse matrices
questions.choice_B: Output sparsity pattern is unknown a priori, requiring dynamic accumulation and possibly more memory traffic
questions.choice_C: SpGEMM cannot be parallelized
questions.choice_D: SpGEMM requires the input matrices to share the same sparsity pattern

questions.question: Which compressed storage format stores all nonzero values and their column indices contiguously per row, along with a row pointer array?
questions.choice_A: COO
questions.choice_B: DOK
questions.choice_C: CSR
questions.choice_D: CSC

questions.question: In CSC (compressed sparse column), which operation is typically more efficient than in CSR?
questions.choice_A: Right-multiplying by a dense vector ($A x$)
questions.choice_B: Row scaling
questions.choice_C: Row-wise iteration
questions.choice_D: Left-multiplying by a dense vector ($A^\top x$) or column-wise operations

questions.question: Why can block-sparse patterns yield better performance on modern hardware compared to purely random sparsity with the same nnz?
questions.choice_A: Block-sparse matrices always have fewer nonzeros than randomly sparse matrices of the same size.
questions.choice_B: Block-sparse patterns allow exact elimination of all memory indirections.
questions.choice_C: Block structure improves spatial locality and enables vectorized/coalesced loads and better use of small dense kernels.
questions.choice_D: Random sparsity cannot be represented in CSR or CSC formats.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of applying a permutation to rows and/or columns of a sparse matrix before computation?
questions.choice_A: It guarantees a reduction in arithmetic complexity for all algorithms.
questions.choice_B: It can expose structure (e.g., banded or block-diagonal) that improves cache locality and reduces fill-in or memory traffic.
questions.choice_C: It converts the matrix to diagonal form without numerical error.
questions.choice_D: It reduces the number of nonzeros without changing the matrix.

questions.question: For SpMV on a multi-core CPU, which partitioning strategy is commonly used to balance load while maintaining locality?
questions.choice_A: Assigning threads to random sets of nonzeros across the matrix
questions.choice_B: Assigning threads to columns uniformly regardless of nnz distribution
questions.choice_C: Assigning threads to contiguous row blocks (or work partitioned by row pointers) with attention to per-block nnz
questions.choice_D: Assigning a single thread to process the entire matrix

questions.question: Which factor most directly limits the performance of SpMV on modern CPUs and GPUs for typical sparsity patterns?
questions.choice_A: Peak floating-point throughput (FLOPs/s)
questions.choice_B: Latency of integer additions in index arithmetic
questions.choice_C: Register file size
questions.choice_D: Memory bandwidth and irregular memory access patterns

questions.question: How does sparsity affect the number of trainable parameters in a neural network layer represented by a weight matrix?
questions.choice_A: The number of trainable parameters equals the total number of entries in the dense weight matrix regardless of sparsity.
questions.choice_B: Only the diagonal entries remain trainable under sparsity constraints.
questions.choice_C: The number of trainable parameters is effectively the number of nonzero entries, possibly plus parameters defining the pattern if it is learned.
questions.choice_D: Sparsity changes the model size but not the degrees of freedom.

questions.question: What is a key trade-off when choosing CSR over COO for runtime computation?
questions.choice_A: CSR uses less memory than COO but cannot represent rectangular matrices.
questions.choice_B: COO supports faster SpMV than CSR due to simpler indexing.
questions.choice_C: CSR improves traversal locality and SpMV speed but makes dynamic insertion and modification of entries more expensive.
questions.choice_D: CSR cannot store duplicate entries while COO must store them.

questions.question: In sparse-sparse matrix multiplication, which high-level accumulation strategy is commonly used to form each output row (or column)?
questions.choice_A: Performing a dense matrix-matrix multiply on zero-padded inputs
questions.choice_B: Sorting all candidate products globally before accumulation
questions.choice_C: Using a sparse accumulator per row, such as a hash table or tree, then compressing to CSR/CSC
questions.choice_D: Computing only diagonal entries and inferring off-diagonals by symmetry

questions.question: Which statement about banded matrices is correct for algorithmic efficiency?
questions.choice_A: Their SpMV cost is $O(n^2)$ due to touching many near-diagonal entries.
questions.choice_B: They are best stored in COO to exploit contiguous memory.
questions.choice_C: Their structure allows $O(nb)$ arithmetic for SpMV with bandwidth $b$, and specialized storage reduces memory traffic.
questions.choice_D: Permutation cannot reduce the bandwidth of a banded matrix.

questions.question: Why might block permutations be applied to a sparse matrix before GPU execution?
questions.choice_A: To convert the matrix into a fully dense block, eliminating sparsity handling
questions.choice_B: To increase the number of nonzeros and thereby improve arithmetic intensity
questions.choice_C: To group nonzeros into block structures that align with warp-level coalesced memory access and shared-memory tiling
questions.choice_D: To force all rows to have identical nnz counts

questions.question: Which storage format often provides the best performance for repeated SpMV with fixed sparsity, assuming row-wise operations dominate?
questions.choice_A: COO due to ease of appending entries
questions.choice_B: CSR due to contiguous storage of row segments and compact row pointers
questions.choice_C: DOK because of dictionary lookups
questions.choice_D: Dense due to vectorization regardless of sparsity

questions.question: As sparsity becomes extreme (very few nonzeros per row), which numerical issue is most likely to emerge in iterative solvers using the matrix?
questions.choice_A: Guaranteed convergence in a fixed number of iterations
questions.choice_B: Underflow in index variables
questions.choice_C: Poor conditioning or loss of diagonal dominance, potentially slowing or preventing convergence
questions.choice_D: Overflow in floating-point multiplication of zeros

questions.question: When comparing storage space versus compute time for sparse formats, which general principle holds?
questions.choice_A: Formats that minimize metadata (indices, pointers) always maximize runtime performance.
questions.choice_B: Denser storage (e.g., blocking) may slightly increase stored values but can significantly reduce runtime by improving locality.
questions.choice_C: The optimal format is independent of the target hardware.
questions.choice_D: Using a dense format is always wasteful for any sparse matrix.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the complexity of sparse-sparse matrix multiplication $C = A B$ in terms of input and output sparsity?
questions.choice_A: It is always $O(\text{nnz}(A) + \text{nnz}(B))$ because only nonzeros are touched once.
questions.choice_B: It is $O(n^3)$ unless both matrices are diagonal.
questions.choice_C: It depends on the structure; a common bound is proportional to the number of scalar products formed (e.g., sum over rows of $A$ of nnz(row)$\times$nnz of corresponding columns in $B$) plus the cost to accumulate and compress the resulting nonzeros.
questions.choice_D: It equals the cost of SpMV with $A$ repeated $n$ times.
